meaningMnemonic: This radical is the same as the kanji. It means bone .

This is a melon . Imagine a melon cut in half, and you're looking at its insides from the side. See those precious private melon parts? You're gonna keep those for yourself, because melons are delicious and not for sharing.
Look at this radical. Can you see it floating in space? Can you see the antennae and reflectors? That's because it's a satellite .
We already have a roof radical, so we're going to use the secondary kanji meaning for this radical. It's shop , remember?

You hit a tree with an axe so you can do some analysis on it. To do the analysis on the tree, a cross section needs to be obtained, so you must chop it in half with your axe. Hints Imagine taking this axe in your hands and chopping away at this tree to do your analysis. Hear the chop chop chop as wood chips fly into your face.
readingMnemonic: The person who is doing this analysis is very sexy ( せき ). Who is this sexy person? Why it’s you of course, you sexy beast. I love watching you do analysis on trees. It’s so sexy. Hints Imagine yourself being sexy and doing tree analysis. What sort of sexy analysis moves can you think of? Oh yeah, so sexy.

meaningMnemonic: Using a bow , shoot a melon and it will fly in a steep arc . Melons are too heavy to fly straight, after all. Hints Imagine shooting a really heavy melon out of a bow. Watch it make an arc through the air. Trace the arc with your finger.
readingMnemonic: Shooting melons in an arc is something little 子 's ( こ ) love to do. It also helps that when they come down from the arc they smash all over the place. Hints Imagine being a 子 and watching melons fly in arcs all over. Imagine a little 子 version of yourself giggling and clapping your hands with absolute glee.

meaningMnemonic: The mole has a knife ready for your arrival . You get out of your airplane, you step on the ground and... ouch! You stepped right on the knife, and there's the mole, sticking it out of the ground. "I checked the schedule for your arrival!" it squeaks happily, and disappears. Hints Welp, your arrival didn't go smoothly. You have a knife in your foot. I'm not sure what you did to make that mole hate you, but you'll have to be more careful next time.
readingMnemonic: Your arrival to とう きょう is now ruined. And your next stop is now going to be an arrival at a とうきょう hospital to get this mole knife out. Hints This certainly wasn't the type of arrival you were expecting when you bought your tickets to とうきょう .

meaningMnemonic: A car works for one reason : its wheels can spin on an axis . Yep, that lateral axis is definitely a car's most pivotal part . Hints Imagine the frustration of trying to drive a car without any axis (or axles) for its wheels to spin on. That thing isn't going anywhere. It's missing its pivotal part!
readingMnemonic: Your friend is always bragging about his car's axis . He's all like, "My car's wheels move on more than one axis!" And you sarcastically reply: " Gee, coo l" ( じく ). Hints The pivotal part your friend leaves out is that those multi-axis wheels are why his car is always crashing. Gee, cool axis control, man.

meaningMnemonic: Shellfish cause landslide s because of all their bustling and lively underwater activity. Hints You ever see cliffs falling into the sea? 99% of those landslides are due to bustling, lively shellfish communities, eroding the base of the cliff with all their hustle and bustle.
readingMnemonic: You can't stand bustling and lively situations, so you get out your knee gui llotine ( にぎ ). What's a knee guillotine? It's exactly what it sounds like, and you're about to use it on these shellfish to prevent some landslides. Hints Any time you're in a bustling place, you reach for your knee guillotine. Imagine, now, the graveyard of shellfish legs that lies before you. Ahh, no more bustle… Also, that's dinner sorted.

meaningMnemonic: When your fingers move like that, you know it's an omen of a challenge that will face you soon in the future. Hints What kind of challenge is it? If you look closely at your fingers sometimes you can figure out the challenge that is to come based on their movements.
readingMnemonic: In your finger, you see a challenge . And... if you look closely, you can see the fast movements of your fingers forming the outline of Mrs. Chou 's ( ちょう ) face. Oh no, the challenge is going to be Mrs. Chou! Hints Whenever you see an omen (radical), there's a good chance that Mrs. Chou will be a part of it. This is not a good sign.

meaningMnemonic: You take a turkey and try to boil it but you char it instead. That's what happens when you throw meat into a pot on high with no water in there. Hints You should know better than to try to boil something without water! Now what are you going to do with this raw, but charred turkey?!
readingMnemonic: You're staring sadly at the char red turkey when you suddenly sense the Shou gun ( しょう ) looming behind you. You were supposed to be cooking this turkey for him and now he looks really, really mad. Hints The Shougun reaches down and bites a charred hunk off the turkey. He yells and spits it out. Why did he do that?! You have no idea but it looked nasty.

meaningMnemonic: You see fingers on a flag by the exit , indicating that you should dig . The fingers on the flag point downward, just by the exit, as if to say "dig here!" There must be something under here. That's what you think to yourself as you start to dig with your fingers. Hints Imagine digging under the flag by the exit of your building with your bare fingers. The dirt is getting under your fingernails as you dig. It's getting on your knees. It's everywhere.
readingMnemonic: You dig until you finally hit something. It's a bunch of buried old coots ( くつ ). They're in an underground room for old coots. One yells up at you, "Whatcha doing to our roof, ya whipper snapper?! Stop digging in our lawn!" Hints You carefully un-dig the old coots and leave them to their old grumpy coot hole... basement... secret clubhouse? Whatever.

meaningMnemonic: Take this thread and look at this part . Now look at this part! Now look at this part. You don't know where to look! Haha, I have distract ed you! Hints You don't know what part of the thread to look at. What a distraction.
readingMnemonic: Despite how distracted you are, that was indeed a lot of fun ( ふん ). Hints Imagine yourself really enjoying looking at parts of the thread. You don't know why it's so fun, but being derpy is exciting, I guess.

meaningMnemonic: This bamboo can be whittled into an example of anything. See, here's a car . Here's a snake . I can make so many examples just with bamboo. Hints It's amazing how fast this guy can whittle!
readingMnemonic: One last example for you. Now I'm going to take this bamboo and whittle it into an example of Han ( はん ) Solo! Hints Han Solo's bamboo example comes to life and runs off.

meaningMnemonic: Someone's fingers touch your tongue and fasten it together. You can't talk. All you can do is make sad tongue-less sounds as you try to figure out who would fasten your tongue like this. Hints Try to fasten your own tongue with your fingers right now. You probably can't do it, right? That's because your fingers are too big and your tongue is too slippery.
readingMnemonic: Only one creature could use its fingers to fasten your tongue like this: cats ( かつ ). Cats are notorious for fastening tongues so that people can't speak. Haven't you ever heard the phrase, "Cat got your tongue?" Hints In this case, many cats fastened your tongue. You should probably be nicer to cats from now on so this doesn't happen again.

meaningMnemonic: You use your fingers in a shop to grip what you want to buy. Hints Imagine picking up a few different things in a shop. If something fits nicely in your grip: buy it. If it's too small or too big, put it back.
readingMnemonic: You have a really strong grip thanks to acu puncture ( あく )! All your fingers are primed for buying things. You can grip anything at a shop—pineapples, tires, even live turtles. All thanks to some well-placed needles. Hints Acupuncture is great for strengthening your grip strength. If you do intense shopping (like I do) you should definitely consider it!

meaningMnemonic: In the tree district of town you can buy a lot of tree products, including doors. With those doors, though, you always need hinge s. Hints Don't forget to buy a hinge. Your door purchase will hinge on your hinges.
readingMnemonic: After you buy it, you need to lubricate your hinge with sou p ( すう ). You've found that soup works better than anything else on the market for keeping your hinges squeak-free and moving smoothly. Hints Different soups work better for different hinges, though. Small cabinet hinge? Try something light and broth-based, like miso soup or consommé. Heavy front door hinge? Go with a thick clam chowder.

meaningMnemonic: If you have fingers it's easy to hoist things above your head. If you don't have fingers, well, it's not so easy. Hints Hoist the sails! Hoist the anchor! Hoist a baby! All of these situations are easier if you have a ton of working fingers. (The more the better.)
readingMnemonic: Today, you have to hoist so much stuff. " Ah ( あ )!" you say, "So much hoisting to do." Better get to it! Hints Imagine hoisting things over and over again. Each time you spot a new thing that needs hoisting, you say "Ah! Something else to hoist!"

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami crashes into the sun (breaking it in half) and creating a different wing of the tsunami all together. This wing crashes down and creates a lagoon . Hints The lagoon is beautiful! The water is hot (from hitting the sun) but it isn't so bright that you'll get a sunburn.
readingMnemonic: This lagoon was created on purpose by a really angry dude and his cata pult ( かた ). He wanted a nice place to lounge that's tropical, but not too bright. So he came up with a plan: use a giant catapult to send a tsunami into the sun! Hints Now picture it all in slow motion. The catapult tosses the tsunami into the air, it smashes the sun, breaks off into a wing of nice, hot water, and finally splashes back to the earth into a beautiful, secluded lagoon.

meaningMnemonic: There are flowers and hills in your front lawn . Your lawn is pretty big and it is covered with both flowers and hills. It’s very pretty. Hints Imagine walking through your lawn and smelling all the flowers as you travel over the rolling hills. What a delightful lawn this is.
readingMnemonic: You are the proud owner of a Shiba ( しば ) Inu, y’know, the Japanese dog? Well, this Shiba Inu of yours loves to run around in your lawn and through the flowers and over the hills. This is the perfect lawn for your Shiba. Hints Look at your little Shiba running through the lawn all happy and elated. Hear him barking as he zooms up and down each hill.

meaningMnemonic: If the moon is dry , it's good for your liver ! Haha, get it? Because there's no moonshine to ruin your liver. Don't drink, kids. Hints Imagine holding an empty bottle up to the moon and seeing it's completely dry. You pat your belly above where your liver is and say, "I guess you're safe tonight, liver."
readingMnemonic: As you pat your liver suddenly a strange feeling bubbles up and the ghost of Genghis Khan ( かん ) comes out! Right out of your liver. Hints Genghis Khan glares down at you, "You inherited my liver, and that means no moonshine for you. Protect your liver and don't drink, like me, Genghis Khan."

meaningMnemonic: What do you eat if you’re wearing horns and surrounded by lantern s? Mochi (or sticky rice cake s) of course! Hints Imagine yourself in the lantern light wearing horns and eating delicious mochi.
readingMnemonic: The reading of mochi is mochi ( もち ). Yay! Hints As long as you can remember the meaning of this kanji, you'll know the reading too.

meaningMnemonic: Under the cross is a mouth and another mouth wearing special clothes because they're in mourning . Hints Picture the cross looming overhead, people's mouths open so they can sob loudly, and everyone wearing the same color clothes (just picture whatever color works for your particular culture/religion combo).
readingMnemonic: As the mourning continues, the sou l ( そう ) of the dead person rises out of the cross. The soul looks around at all of the mourners and nods. Yes, your mourning has pleased it. Hints If you aren't mourning enough, when the soul comes out of the person's body, it will get really mad. "What, I'm not worth a few tears? Really?" And then the soul will haunt you. So you better mourn like you mean it.

meaningMnemonic: Even though you’ve old legs , you overcome your disability. These old legs of yours don’t work very well, but you overcome the odds and you run a marathon! Hints Imagine running a marathon with your old legs to prove you can overcome anything. Feel your old legs cramping up as you try to overcome the marathon and finish the race.
readingMnemonic: When you pass the finish line and finally overcome the limits of your old legs, someone hands you an ice cold Coke ( こく ) as a reward. Mmm, such a refreshing Coke. Hints Filled with the jubilation of achievement from overcoming all odds, imagine the flavor of this cold Coke in your mouth. Fizzy and Coke flavored, it runs down your throat and into your tummy. Yum.

meaningMnemonic: The tsunami that is white is the most scary tsunami of all. It doesn't come in and destroy everything. No, it comes in, goes inside your door, then stays at your place overnight , without even asking! Hints Imagine the white tsunami knocking on your door, walking into your house, and then just laying down on your bed. You try to tell it to leave, but it's a tsunami, and it says it will be staying overnight thank you very much.
readingMnemonic: Your cat walks up to the white tsunami that's staying overnight and decides it doesn't like it, so it hack s ( はく ) up a hairball on it. Even that doesn't get the tsunami to leave. Hints See the hairball slowly sinking into the tsunami. The cat hacks up another one.

meaningMnemonic: If you have one stool and another stool , you have a pair of stools. Look at this pair of stools. Look at it. Hints Imagine being in front of this pair of stools. Picture yourself sitting on one stool, getting up, then sitting on the other. Repeat this process.
readingMnemonic: This pair of stools shares a sou l ( そう ). Even if you tried to separate them, they'd eventually find their way back together. Hints It's the same with pairs of socks and pairs of people. Sometimes what looks like two things is really a perfect pair, with one soul. Meant to be together forever.

meaningMnemonic: You walk up to a tree and put dynamite on it. Then you set it off. BOOM. It explodes, but doesn't do what you'd expect. Instead of blowing the tree up, it blasts a very beautiful pattern into the side of it as well as the ground around it. Hints Think about what pattern it might be. Is it a checkered pattern? Something more complicated and beautiful? Whatever it is, think of something that really impresses you.
readingMnemonic: The pattern is so beautiful that you want to put it on your gara ge ( がら ). So, you do. Hints Imagine painting your garage with the pattern you imagined earlier.

meaningMnemonic: Wrap your fingers around this axe and put it in your mouth to express your philosophy . Your philosophy of… putting axes in your mouth. Everyone else seems to think it's a stupid philosophy, but by doing this you're showing them that it's not! Hints Imagine expressing your philosophy, your deepest thoughts and beliefs, by putting an axe in your mouth. Is it some kind of metaphor for how powerful and sharp your philosophical thinking is?
readingMnemonic: Your axe-in-mouth philosophy means you're always tasting 鉄 ( てつ ). They say blood tastes like copper. Well, weapons (and your philosophy) taste like iron. Hints Your philosophy and your way of life means everything tastes like 鉄 now, and you think everyone should be that way.

meaningMnemonic: Use simultaneous jackhammer s to perform the purification ritual. Two jackhammers running perfectly in sync will purify your body, mind, and soul! (And the ground around you that's being jackhammered.) Hints Close your eyes and feel the purification begin. Try not to let the loud jackhammering sound bother you, just focus on the simultaneous vibrations cleansing you inside and out.
readingMnemonic: This purification ritual is supposed to help you forget your cy borg ( さい ). It's been a while, but you can't seem to get it out of your head. Hints Hopefully this purification (or just the two jackhammers shaking your brain up like pudding) will get the memories of your cyborg to go away. You can't keep picturing it all the time like this.

meaningMnemonic: If you take a thread and wrap up a bunch of it, so much it becomes a hill of thread, you're going to have a lot of thread. You can wrap some of that thread around other thread to create a much thicker thread. This thread is a rope . Hints Imagine yourself twisting this hill of thread up to make thicker ropes. They're strong!
readingMnemonic: Congratulations, now you have a perfect rope for tuna ( つな ) fishing. Tunas are massive, so you need a strong rope to reel one in. Hints Imagine yourself going tuna fishing on a small boat with nothing but one long rope. This is how tuna fishing is done where you're from, so you're sticking to tradition.

meaningMnemonic: You keep your substitute clothes in a sack . The clothes in the sack are just substitute clothes, so they only come out in emergencies. Hints Look at this sack of substitute clothes. Imagine it filled with all the clothes you hardly ever wear. What kind of clothes would be inside this sack?
readingMnemonic: You need your substitute clothes so you take out your substitute clothes sack . You open it up to grab your substitute clothes, only to find out that there is a ton of salmon roe inside your sack. Oh man, you forgot all about putting that in there. You yell: F**K ROE ( ふくろ ) because that roe destroyed all your clothes and made it nasty. Hints Imagine how nasty it is in there. Also imagine how smelly it is. Feel angry about putting roe in your sack. Why would you even do that? Why would the roe do this to you, as well.

meaningMnemonic: With your fingers , you grab a satellite and shake it! You're an astronaut and it's your job. Don't worry, the satellite won't break or anything, it's strong enough for space travel. Just do as you're told and shake the sucker. Hints Imagine being in space and shaking a satellite with your fingers.
readingMnemonic: You need to shake it because this satellite is full of yo gurt ( よう ). You only like yogurt that's been well shaken. And who can resist space yogurt? Huh? Anyone? Hints Imagine shaking yogurt in space. Now imagine eating yogurt as it continues to shake (in space still)!

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami breaks your bone s, not from hitting you, but from making you slide and slip into stuff. Hard to keep your footing in a tsunami, you know? You're slipping and sliding all over the place. Hints Imagine being knocked off your feet by a tsunami, then sliding into a wall or something and breaking a bone or two. You try to get up, but you slip again, breaking a few more bones in the process.
readingMnemonic: As you continue to slide around you see a bunch of stray cats ( かつ ) slipping and sliding too. They're yowling and sliding right toward you. Uh oh… Hints Picture these stray cats trying to right themselves on the wet ground and slipping again each time. They're doing that thing cats do when they touch water, twisting their bodies around and trying to cling to you. Great, now you've got a bunch of slippery cats perched atop your broken body.

meaningMnemonic: A servant secures a stool in the dirt so that it is a solid sitting device. If you just throw a stool on the ground it will flop over easily. But if you have a servant to dig it into the dirt a bit, it becomes nice and solid and safe for sitting! Hints Picture two stools in your mind. One is solid, you want to sit on it. The other looks like the wind will knock it over. Don't sit on that!
readingMnemonic: You need this stool to be extra solid because you're using it to test your new cata pult ( かた ). If it isn't solid, when you launch it and yourself in the catapult, the stool might fall over, killing you both. And you don't want that, now do you? Hints You better hope that catapult is solid too. If it isn't the whole thing will come apart when you try to launch yourself into the air.

meaningMnemonic: You hop in your car with an axe and drive to the sun , but you'll only be there temporarily . You offed someone with your axe, and you're fleeing to the sun to lie low temporarily while the cops search for you. Hints After hiding out temporarily on the sun for a few days, you'll dispose of your axe in the raging inferno there and then drive your car back to Earth like nothing happened. It's the perfect plan.
readingMnemonic: Apparently you took a wrong turn, and the place you temporarily hid out was Zan zibar ( ざん ) — not the sun. Zanzibar is also super hot and sunny, so you can be forgiven for making this mistake. Hints You actually really enjoyed temporarily staying in Zanzibar. The beaches were amazing, and the miles of coastline made it really easy to dispose of your axe.

meaningMnemonic: Thread and vines alone are too weak to hold anything up, but if you twist together both of them, you can make something much stronger. Hints As you twist together endless strands of thread and vines, feel how tough and sturdy your makeshift rope is beginning to get. You could swing through the jungle like Tarzan on this thing.
readingMnemonic: As you twist together the thread and vines, you suddenly feel a lump. You look down and see a cu cumber ( きゅう ) twisted into it. Hints It turns out those vines you've been twisting together are cucumber vines, so if you need a break to rest your hands, you can chow down on a healthy and refreshing cucumber while you recover.

meaningMnemonic: You gaze at flowers as you meet your death beside a river out in the wild . You wandered off into a wild part of nature, but your subpar survival skills have led you to your death. At least you have some pretty flowers and a nice river to look at as you kick the bucket in this wild, wild wilderness. Hints Imagine how the flowers smell and what the river sounds like as you lie there, death approaching. Being out here in such a wild place, you feel really in tune with nature and the planet — maybe this isn't such a bad way to go.
readingMnemonic: Just as the wild wilderness is about to claim you, you see a familiar face. " Ah ( あ ), you cry wildly, Ala ddin ( あら )!" Yes, your good buddy Aladdin has flown in on his magic carpet to save you from your death in this wild and remote place. Hints "Ah, Aladdin, I knew you'd come for me," you say as he loads your feeble body onto his magic carpet. He smiles back at you and says, "Come on, buddy. Let's get you someplace a little less wild so you can rest and recuperate."

meaningMnemonic: A challenge for war ? This is a challenge worth accepting. After all, we can't give up without at least giving it a try or making some kind of an attempt . Note that 挑戦 refers to a challenge not in the sense of a difficult, challenging task, but in the sense of a bold or daring attempt to take on that task — whether that's defeating a formidable foe, performing an impressive feat, or tackling a tricky problem.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.english: I thought something was wrong with the car, and sure enough, they found a problem with the wheel's central axis area.

sentences.english: How you live changes depending on what you choose to center your life around.

sentences.english: Hmm, in this machine, the central axis here might be a little off.Even a slight wobble in the axis can throw off the balance of the whole thing.

sentences.english: Last night I had a dream about a coral polyp's axial skeleton.

meaningMnemonic: Something that is transparent enough for things (like light) to pass through is going to be transparent . In other words, it's going to be clear or to be translucent . Unlike 透ける , which just focuses on something being "see-through," 透き通る describes something as having a remarkably clear, transparent, or translucent quality. While it's commonly used for things like glass and water, you may also see it used to describe someone's voice or a cloudless sky as a way of poetically emphasizing their beautifully clear or pure quality.
readingMnemonic: The readings for this word are both kun'yomi readings. You've learned both of these readings by now so you should be able to read this on your own.

readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already when you learned 漬ける , so you should be able to read this one too.

meaningMnemonic: You know that 吹く is "to blow" and that 飛ばす is "To let fly." So, if you use your blowing to let something fly, you are going to blow away it.
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 吹く and 飛ばす , put together.

sentences.english: Let’s go to the party and brush off your depression.

meaningMnemonic: You know that 吹く is "to blow" and the kanji 込 means into . So this word means to blow in or to breathe into , and it can be used both transitively and intransitively. It can also be used figuratively to mean to breathe into or to imbue , like breathing new life into something, or imbuing someone’s mind with hatred.
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from the word 吹く and the kanji 込む .

sentences.japanese: 家はおんぼろで、嵐が来る度に雨風が吹き込むのが現実です。
sentences.english: The reality is that the house is so old that the rain and wind blows in whenever a storm comes.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with a う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means challenge , and the verb form means to challenge someone or to take on something difficult . 挑む is a relatively formal word for boldly facing a challenge. It has a strong, spirited feel, like a climber saying "I'm taking on Mt. Everest!" You'll come across it in headlines, live sports commentary, anime battle scenes, or even in daily life when someone wants to sound determined and fired up about their big personal goal.
readingMnemonic: I do n't ( いど ) just challenge anyone, but when I challenge someone, it's for real. My challenging reflexes come from my Id ( いど ), after all.

sentences.english: He challenged the king to battle.

sentences.japanese: 私はこの日曜日、有名なベーコン鑑定家に挑みます。
sentences.english: I'm going to challenge the famous bacon connoisseur this Sunday.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means hoist . But most commonly (and most importantly), this word means to deep fry . I guess you can think of it as hoisting that delicious deep-fried food out of the oil. Of course, 揚げる can also mean to hoist (a sail) or to raise (a flag) depending on the context.
readingMnemonic: Remember the other "to raise" vocabs? They are all あげる as well. For example, 上げる is あげる and 挙げる is あげる as well.

meaningMnemonic: You've already learned one verb for this kanji: 薄まる (to be diluted). Well, this is its transitive sibling, so it means to dilute or to water down something. Here, you're the one actively thinning something down.
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 薄い , so if you know that you'll be able to read this too.

sentences.japanese: この味噌汁はしょっぱすぎるよ。もうちょっと薄めてもらってもいいかな？

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means distract and the verb vocab version of this word is to distract or to divert . 紛らす generally refers to trying to take your mind off negative things like boredom, pain, sadness, or stress, as in 気を紛らす (to distract yourself) or 痛みを紛らす (to take your mind off the pain). You're not removing the problem itself, just giving your brain something else to focus on so you can forget about it for a little while.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: When you want to distract yourself from all your troubles, you hang out with your pal Maggie ( まぎ ). Maggie's the most awesome person you know, and being around her always helps you to divert yourself from life's problems. Thanks for being such a great shoulder to lean on, Maggie!

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means char , but the verb version is to get burned , to get scorched , or to get charred . This is for when something is burned on the surface. Most of the time, 焦げる is the unhappy and accidental kind of burning. You can use 焦げる when your bread is burned in the toaster, for example, or a shirt is scorched and blackened by an iron.
readingMnemonic: The times where you were burned were mostly when you were a 子 ( こ ). That's because kids aren't good at working with hot things.

sentences.english: My mom said that you can prevent the bottom of the pan from getting burned by stirring consistently.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means grip and the verb vocab version is to grasp .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You go to grasp someone. You really need them. You are soooo needy ( にぎ ). Except, you can't really pronounce "d" sounds very well, so you say にぎ .

sentences.japanese: おにぎりは、ご飯を握って作るので「お握り」と呼ばれています。

meaningMnemonic: The kanji itself means lack , and this verb means to lack something . 欠く is often used for intangible qualities someone lacks, like flexibility or consideration. But it can also be used for physical things, especially in the context of basic necessities. It sounds kind of advanced and formal, so it tends to pop up more in writing than in casual speech. Note that this is a transitive verb, so it takes a direct object — someone is actively lacking something, like あの人の行動は常識を欠いている (their behavior lacks common sense).
readingMnemonic: If your life seems to lack something , like excitement or meaning, the best thing you can do is hop in your ca r ( か ). Take your car out on the open road and go search for whatever it is you're lacking. You'll find it — we believe in you!

meaningMnemonic: You know how 逃げる means "to escape"? This is the transitive version, so it means to let someone escape , to let someone go , or to set someone free . You know this because you'd want to let everyone escape when the place is filled with gas ( がす ). 逃がす is often about purposely letting someone or something go — like setting a bird free or letting a captive escape quietly. But it can also be used in more unintentional and regretful situations, like failing to catch a criminal or missing a big opportunity.
readingMnemonic: You learned the に reading for this kanji when you learned 逃げる but here’s another mnemonic to help you remember: You decided to let someone escape because they were on their knee s ( に ) begging you to set them free.

meaningMnemonic: 駆ける is "to gallop" and the kanji 込 means into . To gallop into a place is to rush into it. You can’t gallop slowly, after all. This can also mean to seek refuge , as in hurrying to a place for safety and support.
readingMnemonic: The readings come from 駆ける and 込む .

readingMnemonic: If everything starts to shake what else will shake along with it? You ( ゆ ), of course.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means slide and the verb vocab version is to slide , to slip , or to glide . 滑る is a versatile word that can cover all kinds of actions, like sliding down playground slides, slipping on ice, skiing or skating, and even failing a test or being demoted.
readingMnemonic: You're about to slip , and notice the floor is covered entirely in souve nirs ( すべ )! Souvenirs of all shapes and sizes are scattered all over the floor, making it extremely easy to slide and slip.

meaningMnemonic: You know 駆ける is "to gallop" and 出す is "to let out." Well, in order to gallop off and let yourself out of somewhere, you're going to need to start running first. Fundamentally, 駆け出す just describes the act of beginning to run, but it's often used to mean to rush out of somewhere. For example, schoolchildren might 駆け出す out of their classroom and make a beeline for the playground when they hear the bell ring.
readingMnemonic: The readings come from 駆ける and 出す .

sentences.japanese: 彼に質問を尋ねた時、駆け出しただけだ。
sentences.english: When I asked him a question he just ran off.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means overnight and the verb vocab version is to stay the night .

You'll often see this activity in the 運動会 (sports day) event in Japanese schools.

readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: アヤの最新のトーフグキャラのイラストは、とても躍動感に溢れています。
sentences.english: Aya’s latest illustration of the Tofugu characters is very vibrant and lively.

meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of wild ? It's wild or rough .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned two kun'yomi readings for this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: You know who's really wild ? Ala ddin ( あら ). He's always doing wild things like overthrowing evil viziers or zipping around the skies on his magic carpet. Yep, no one's wilder than that wily street urchin Aladdin.

sentences.japanese: 私の初めての彼氏はいつも鼻が詰まっていて、電話をする時は息づかいが荒かったです。
sentences.english: My first boyfriend always had a stuffy nose and would breathe hard when we talked on the phone.
